data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Basal cell carcinoma** (Premalignant & malignant tumours)_

**Q1. Define BCC.**
- Commonest skin (and human) cancer — slow-growing, locally invasive malignant tumour arising from basaloid cells of the epidermis/follicular stem cells; rarely metastasises (<0.1%) but can destroy local tissues ('rodent ulcer')
- In India: commoner than SCC on face; pigmented BCC is the predominant type in Indian skin

**Q2. Discuss risk factors (PYQ).**
- UV radiation (intermittent intense exposure, childhood sunburns), fair skin/Fitzpatrick I–II, light eyes, freckling, older age, male
- Ionising radiation, arsenic (wells, Fowler's solution — multiple trunk BCCs), immunosuppression (transplant), PUVA, previous BCC
- Genetic: basal cell naevus syndrome (Gorlin — PTCH1), xeroderma pigmentosum, Bazex–Dupré–Christol, Rombo syndrome, albinism, nevus sebaceous (trichoblastoma more often)
- Molecular: Hedgehog pathway activation — PTCH1 loss or SMO activation (>90%), p53 mutations (UV signature)

**Q3. Describe the clinical types.**
- Nodular (commonest ~50%): pearly translucent papule/nodule with rolled border, arborising telangiectasia, central ulceration ('rodent ulcer') — face (inner canthus, nasolabial fold, nose)
- Pigmented nodular (common in Indians — brown-black, mimics melanoma)
- Superficial (trunk — red scaly plaque with thread-like pearly border, multicentric)
- Morphoeic/infiltrative/sclerosing (ivory scar-like plaque, ill-defined, aggressive, high recurrence)
- Micronodular, basosquamous (metatypical — more aggressive, can metastasise), cystic, fibroepithelioma of Pinkus (pink pedunculated lower back)
- Write a short note on multicentric (superficial) BCC (PYQ): multiple foci within one lesion; on trunk; suitable for topical/cryotherapy/PDT

**Q4. Discuss the HPE of BCC (PYQ).**
- Nests and islands of basaloid cells with scanty cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei, peripheral palisading, retraction artefact (clefts between tumour and mucinous stroma), mitoses and apoptotic cells, myxoid stroma; connection to epidermis
- Variants: nodular (large nests), superficial (buds from the epidermis), micronodular, infiltrative/morphoeic (thin cords in sclerotic stroma), keratotic, adenoid, pigmented, basosquamous
- Immunohistochemistry: BerEP4 positive (vs SCC negative), Bcl-2 diffuse, CK5/6

**Q5. Dermoscopy.**
- Arborising (tree-like branching) vessels, blue-grey ovoid nests and globules, leaf-like structures, spoke-wheel areas, ulceration, shiny white structures; absence of pigment network

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Nodular: intradermal naevus, sebaceous hyperplasia, molluscum, keratoacanthoma/SCC, amelanotic melanoma, adnexal tumours (trichoepithelioma)
- Pigmented: melanoma, seborrhoeic keratosis, blue naevus
- Superficial: Bowen's, psoriasis, eczema, AK, tinea
- Morphoeic: scar, morphoea
- Ulcerated: SCC, chronic infections (lupus vulgaris, leishmaniasis)

**Q7. Discuss the management of BCC (PYQ).**
- Risk stratification (NCCN): high-risk — location (H-zone of face: central face, eyelids, eyebrows, nose, lips, chin, ear, temple; hands, feet, genitals), size ≥2 cm on trunk/limbs, ill-defined border, recurrent, immunosuppression, prior radiotherapy, aggressive histology (morphoeic, infiltrative, micronodular, basosquamous), perineural invasion
- Surgery (gold standard): standard excision with 4 mm margins (low-risk) / wider for high-risk; Mohs micrographic surgery — highest cure (~99% primary) for high-risk and facial/recurrent BCC (tissue sparing with complete margin control)
- Destructive (low-risk, superficial/small nodular): curettage and electrodesiccation, cryosurgery, photodynamic therapy, CO2 laser
- Topical (superficial BCC): imiquimod 5% (5 times/week for 6 weeks), 5-FU 5% (twice daily for 3–6 weeks)
- Radiotherapy: elderly/inoperable, as adjuvant after incomplete excision; avoid in Gorlin syndrome (induces new BCCs)
- Advanced/metastatic: Hedgehog pathway inhibitors — vismodegib, sonidegib (SMO inhibitors; side effects — muscle cramps, dysgeusia, alopecia, weight loss, teratogenicity); cemiplimab (anti-PD-1) after HHI failure
- Follow-up yearly (≥5 years) — 40% develop another BCC; sun protection

**Q8. Describe the role of cryosurgery for BCC (PYQ).**
- For low-risk, well-defined superficial or small nodular BCC on trunk/limbs, elderly or poor surgical candidates
- Liquid nitrogen (−196 °C) open spray with 3–5 mm margin, double freeze–thaw cycle (tissue temperature ≤ −50 °C), thaw time ≥60–90 s; cure rates ~90–95% in selected tumours
- Advantages: quick, cheap, office procedure, safe in pacemaker/anticoagulated patients; disadvantages: no histological margin control, hypopigmentation, scarring, oedema, delayed healing; avoid for morphoeic, recurrent, H-zone deep tumours

**Q9. What is Mohs micrographic surgery?**
- Staged excision with horizontal frozen sections examining 100% of the peripheral and deep margin, mapped and re-excised only where tumour remains — maximal cure with maximal tissue preservation; indications — high-risk BCC/SCC, recurrent tumours, facial sites, ill-defined/aggressive histology, DFSP, extramammary Paget's, lentigo maligna (modified)

**Q10. Write short notes on nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin) (PYQ).**
- Autosomal dominant PTCH1 (also PTCH2, SUFU) — Hedgehog pathway
- Multiple BCCs from childhood/adolescence (also non-sun-exposed), odontogenic keratocysts of jaw, palmar/plantar pits, calcification of falx cerebri, bifid/fused/splayed ribs, frontal bossing, macrocephaly, hypertelorism, medulloblastoma (SUFU — childhood), ovarian/cardiac fibromas, milia, epidermoid cysts
- Management: avoid radiation (including CT where possible), sun protection, regular skin checks, early treatment of BCCs (Mohs, PDT, topical), vismodegib for multiple; dental panoramic X-rays for jaw cysts; genetic counselling

**Q11. Write short notes on fibroepithelioma of Pinkus (PYQ — epithelioma).**
- Variant of BCC: sessile/pedunculated pink fleshy plaque on lower back resembling fibroma/skin tag; histology — thin anastomosing strands of basaloid cells in fibrous stroma (fenestrated pattern); excision curative

## Quick spotter facts
- Pearly nodule with rolled edge and arborising vessels at inner canthus — BCC
- Peripheral palisading + retraction clefts
- Pigmented BCC common in Indians; Mohs for H-zone

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Basal cell carcinoma); NCCN risk stratification. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
